name: The Mamluk Sultanate
title: Social Hierarchy of the Mamluk Sultanate: From Sultan to Enslaved
in: the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and Syria
period: 1250–1517 (the Bahri and Burji sultans of Egypt and Syria)

tiers.name: The sultan
tiers.you: You were bought as a slave boy and now rule Egypt and Syria from the Citadel of Cairo, but you keep the throne only as long as the amirs and your own royal mamluks stay loyal.
tiers.kid: Many Mamluk sultans had been bought as slave boys and trained as soldiers before they rose to the throne.
tiers.rise: No fixed rule decided the succession: an amir with enough mamluks behind him could seize the throne, as Baybars did in 1260 and Barquq in 1382, and a sultan who lost the amirs’ support could be deposed or killed.
tiers.why: The sultan ruled Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz from the Citadel of Cairo.

tiers.name: Amirs
tiers.term: amir, amir mi'a (of a hundred), amir tablkhana (of forty), amir 'ashara (of ten)
tiers.you: You command your own mamluks as an amir of forty and live on the revenues of lands assigned to you, but your iqta is not yours to pass on, and a turn of faction could cost you everything.
tiers.kid: Amirs were the top army commanders, paid with the taxes from lands the sultan assigned to them.
tiers.rise: A mamluk became an amir by the sultan’s favour after years of service and might climb from ten to forty to a hundred; at the top an amir could make himself sultan. A fall from favour could bring imprisonment, the confiscation of his wealth and death.
tiers.why: The amirs were the senior mamluks, the commanders and governors of the realm.

tiers.name: Mamluk soldiers
tiers.term: mamluk (pl. mamalik), al-mamalik al-sultaniyya (the royal mamluks)
tiers.you: You were bought as a boy from beyond the Black Sea, raised in the barracks of the Citadel and then freed; now you ride in the sultan’s regiments, a free Muslim soldier of the ruling caste.
tiers.kid: Mamluks were boys bought as slaves and trained as soldiers, then set free to serve their masters in the army.
tiers.rise: A mamluk rose by his master’s favour, from trooper to amir and sometimes to sultan; when a new sultan came to power, the mamluks of his predecessors could find themselves pushed aside. His own sons were born free and Muslim, and so were mostly barred from following him into the caste.
tiers.why: The mamluks were the free soldiers of the ruling caste, men who had begun life as slaves.

tiers.name: Sons of mamluks
tiers.you: You are the son of an amir, born free and Muslim, and for that very reason barred from the mamluk regiments; you study with the scholars of Cairo and may make your name in the administration or as a historian.
tiers.kid: Sons of mamluks were born free, so most could not join the soldier class; many became scholars instead.
tiers.rise: A father’s wealth and connections gave them a start, and a sultan’s son might be set on the throne as a figurehead, but the rank their fathers held could not be inherited.
tiers.why: The sons of mamluks, the awlad al-nas, were the paradox at the heart of the system.

tiers.name: Scholars and judges
tiers.you: You teach law in a madrasa endowed by an amir and may one day sit as a judge, but your post depends on the sultan’s favour.
tiers.kid: Muslim scholars called ulama worked as judges and teachers, and people looked to them for guidance.
tiers.rise: Learning was open to any free Muslim man, and scholars rose by study, patronage and appointment: Ibn Khaldun, a newcomer from Tunis, served in Cairo as Maliki chief judge.
tiers.why: The ulama, the scholars of Islamic law and religion, led the civilian population and stood between it and its rulers.

tiers.name: Officials and scribes
tiers.you: You draft the sultan’s letters in the chancery or keep the accounts of a treasury; if you are a Copt, the next riot could cost you your post unless you convert.
tiers.kid: Scribes wrote the sultan’s letters and kept the government’s accounts, and many of them were Christians.
tiers.rise: Skill and patronage carried a scribe up the bureaus; for a Coptic scribe, conversion to Islam was often the price of keeping his career.

tiers.name: Townspeople
tiers.you: You keep a shop or work at a craft in the crowded markets of Cairo, rent rooms in an apartment block above the storerooms, and pay the taxes that needy sultans keep raising.
tiers.kid: Cairo was one of the biggest cities in the world, full of merchants, shopkeepers and craftspeople.
tiers.rise: Trade could make a fortune, and the plagues, which left fewer hands, improved the lot of the craftsmen who survived; confiscation, debt or a sultan’s monopoly could ruin a merchant.
tiers.why: Merchants, shopkeepers, craftsmen and labourers filled the towns.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You farm the land along the Nile with your family and hand over a share of every crop to the amir who holds your village’s revenue as his iqta, fearing the plague and the Bedouin raids.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers, and in Egypt their fields were watered by the Nile’s yearly flood.
tiers.rise: Flight to the towns, easier once the plagues had emptied them, was the usual way off the land.
tiers.why: Most of the sultanate’s people were peasants: the fellahin of the Nile valley and Delta and the villagers of Syria and Palestine.

tiers.name: Christians and Jews
tiers.you: You are a Copt who pays the jizya, wears the dress the law prescribes and may not ride even a donkey in town, and your church could be shut after the next riot; converting to Islam would free you of all of it.
tiers.kid: Christians and Jews could keep their religions but paid a special tax and had to follow extra rules.
tiers.rise: Conversion to Islam ended the jizya and the restrictions at once and saved a scribe’s career; so many Copts took that road that by 1517 Muslims may have outnumbered Christians in Egypt by ten to one.
tiers.why: Christians and Jews lived as dhimmis, protected but subordinate.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.term: ʿabd (slave), jariya (slave woman), umm walad, tawashi (eunuch)
tiers.you: You were sold as a girl in a slave market and now cook and clean in an amir’s household; if your master takes you as a concubine and acknowledges your child, you can no longer be sold.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay, most of them as household servants.
tiers.rise: A slave could be freed by an owner or agree a contract to buy his freedom with his own earnings, and an umm walad was freed at her master’s death. Khawand Tughay, bought as a slave by al-Nasir Muhammad, was freed and married by him.
tiers.why: Apart from the boys bought to become mamluks, slaves in the sultanate served mostly in households, and women always outnumbered men among them.
